investigacion.base:
I couldn't open the Barchart CBZ26 page or the Metaculus FAQ directly, so I can't tell you what either one shows today. Everything below comes from secondary sources dated October 18–19, 2026.

**Where the price is now (Oct 19, 2026)**
- Brent fell sharply on Monday. One report has it down 2.48% to US$107.13 a barrel, shedding US$2.73. Investing.com showed the Dec-26 contract (LCOZ6) at about 108.10, previous close 109.86, day's range 106.83–109.34, 52-week range 58.72–126.41.
- One contract detail matters a lot here: Investing.com lists the Dec-26 Settlement Day: 10/30/2026. That means CBZ26 is still the front month on Oct 29 but trades in its second-to-last session that day. Prices can get choppy or squeezed right before a physically settled contract expires.

**What's driving it**
- The drop was blamed on Trump's decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia.
- Pushing the other way: on Friday it briefly touched US$110, its highest since May, after a week of attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) is still attacking ships there (Invezz, Oct 18).
- How 2026 got here: Brent rose from US$61 at the start of the year to US$118 by the end of March. It then fell to US$72 by 1 July after a June agreement lifted Hormuz flows. After that came attacks on Saudi pumping stations, a US blockade of Iranian exports and the 11 September bombing of a Saudi pipeline, and Brent climbed back above US$100.
- OPEC+: On 4 October the core group kept November output targets unchanged, having already signalled a pause in quota increases until the end of 2026.
- Forecasts: Goldman Sachs estimates spot Brent carries a risk premium of nearly US$25 a barrel. The EIA sees Brent averaging US$105 in Q4; Goldman expects US$90 in December. Trading Economics' model projects 113.86 by quarter-end.

**How much it could move (my rough estimate)**
- Assuming implied volatility of about 40–50% a year, given the recent geopolitical swings, 8 trading days works out to a one-standard-deviation move of roughly ±7–8%, or about ±$8. Recent single-day moves of 2–2.5% are consistent with that.
- Tail risks: worse Hormuz escalation could push it toward the 52-week high around $126. A ceasefire or a jump in Russian exports could knock out much of the risk premium, as happened in June when prices fell sharply.

**Events before Oct 29**
- Weekly EIA inventory reports (Oct 21 and Oct 28).
- Ongoing news on Hormuz, Iran, Saudi infrastructure and the Russia sanctions waiver.
- The Dec contract expires Oct 30.
- I didn't find any OPEC+ meeting scheduled before Oct 29.

**Status quo:** If the question resolved today, the answer would be about **107–108**.

I didn't check prediction markets, so I have no prices to cite from them.

**Sources:**
- [1](https://kalkine.com.au/news/economic-news/brent-crude-price-2026-up-76-why-the-hormuz-crisis-still-outweighs-a-russia-sanctions-waiver)
- [2](https://www.investing.com/commodities/brent-oil)
- [3](https://tradingeconomics.com/commodity/brent-crude-oil)

criterios: This question resolves to the official settlement price (in USD per barrel) of the ICE Brent Crude front-month futures contract on October 29, 2026, as reported on the Barchart historical-price page for the December 2026 contract (CBZ26): https://www.barchart.com/futures/quotes/CBZ26/price-history/historical . The resolution value is the "Last" (settlement) price shown in the row dated 10/29/2026. For example, a settlement of $104.37 resolves as 104.37. If Barchart does not report a settlement for that date, the question resolves to the ICE Brent front-month settlement for October 29, 2026 as reported by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions).
letra_pequena: The front-month contract is the nearest-to-expiry ICE Brent Crude futures contract; as of the resolution date this is the December 2026 contract (CBZ26). If October 29, 2026 is a trading holiday or the market does not settle that day, the most recent prior trading day's settlement in October 2026 is used. If the ICE Brent futures contract ceases to settle or the metric is no longer published anywhere, the question is annulled.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** 10 calendar days, about 8 trading sessions. The outcome will be known at settlement on October 29, 2026, which is the December contract's second-to-last session before its October 30 expiry.

(b) **If nothing changed:** about $107–108. This is the December contract's level after Monday's roughly 2.5% drop on the Russia sanctions/tariff waiver.

(c) **If the current trend continued:** The trend is mixed. Prices rose to $110 on the Hormuz tanker attacks, then fell back on the Russia waiver. Since early October the drift has been mildly upward, from about $100 to $106–110. Continuing that drift points to roughly $108–112. Continuing the latest pullback points to the low $100s.

(d) **Experts and markets:**
- The EIA sees Q4 averaging about $105.
- Goldman expects $90 in December and estimates a risk premium of about $25.
- Trading Economics' model projects about $114 by quarter-end.
- Implied volatility of roughly 40–50% gives a one-standard-deviation move of about ±$8 over 8 sessions.
- Fundamentals (the IEA stock release, the possible easing of sanctions on Iranian, Russian and Venezuelan oil, a $25 risk premium) lean slightly bearish. Geopolitics leans bullish.

(e) **Low scenario:** A Hormuz de-escalation or ceasefire, similar to June's agreement, removes much of the risk premium. Add the Russia waiver boosting flows and broader sanctions easing on shadow-fleet vessels, and Brent could drop to the $85–95 range within days.

(f) **High scenario:** A major IRGC escalation, such as a tanker sinking, a closure attempt, or another strike on Saudi infrastructure, could coincide with a squeeze near expiry on the physically settled December contract. That could push the price to $120–126 or beyond.

My median is about $106, a little below the current price, reflecting the slight bearish tilt from fundamentals. I widened the tails beyond the ±$8 one-standard-deviation band to allow for geopolitical shocks and pre-expiry choppiness.

(a) **Time left:** Ten calendar days, including eight scheduled trading sessions, until the October 29 settlement.

(b) **If nothing changed:** The settlement would be around **$107–$108/bbl**, near the reported October 19 price.

(c) **If the latest trend continued:** Repeating Monday’s roughly 2.5% daily decline through October 29 would put it near **$87/bbl**. That is a trend extrapolation, not my central forecast.

(d) **Experts and markets:** The cited EIA forecast of about **$105/bbl for Q4** supports a price near today’s level. Goldman’s **$90 December** expectation points lower, while the cited Trading Economics quarter-end projection points higher. None fixes a price for this particular day.

(e) **Unexpected low scenario:** A durable easing of Hormuz tensions, alongside substantially greater sanctioned-oil supply, could take the settlement into the **$80s**.

(f) **Unexpected high scenario:** A serious disruption to shipping or oil infrastructure could push it **above $125/bbl**.
